{{Short description|Operator on a Hilbert space that shifts basis vectors}}
In [[operator theory]], the '''unilateral shift''' is a one-sided [[shift operator]], that is, a shift operator acting on one-sided [[sequence]]s or [[shift space]]s. The term "[[operator (mathematics)|operator]]" is used to draw contrast to finite-dimensional [[shift matrix|shift matrices]]. The term "unilateral" draws a distinction to the [[bilateral shift operator]], of which the [[Baker's map]] is an example.

Shift operators are commonly studied in the context of [[measure-preserving dynamical system]]s. In such general settings, the unilateral shift operator is usually called the [[transfer operator]] or the Frobenius-Peron operator; its inverse is the [[Koopman operator]]. The properties of shift operators depend very strongly on the [[topology]] of the spaces on which they act; for example, the [[Bernoulli shift]] famously has a [[discrete spectrum]] given by the [[Bernoulli polynomial]]s when acting on the space of bounded [[smooth function]]s on the unit interval, but has a continuous spectrum (on the unit disk), when acting on the Hilbert space of square-integrable functions. When acting on a [[measure space]], the eigenfunctions of shift operators are characteristically fractal in shape, often differentiable-nowhere or even continuous-nowhere. Eigenvalues on the unit circle are associated with [[unitary operator|unitary]] time evolution, while those inside the unit disk are conventionally identified with [[dissipative system|decaying mode]]s in statistical systems. In [[quantum mechanics]], the prototypical unilateral shift operator is the [[annihilation operator]] of the [[quantum harmonic oscillator]]; it's eigenfunctions correspond to [[coherent state]]s.

This article deals primarily with unilateral shifts acting on [[Hilbert space]], specifically in two representations: as an operator on the [[ℓp space|sequence space]] <math>\ell^2</math>, or as a multiplication operator on a [[Hardy space]]. Its properties, particularly its [[invariant subspace]]s, are well-understood and serve as a model for more general theories.<ref name="GMR2023" >{{Harvard citation|Garcia|Mashreghi|Ross|2023}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Holub |first1=JR. |title=On Shift Operators |journal=Canadian Mathematical Bulletin |year=1988 |volume=31 |issue=1 |pages=85–94 |doi=10.4153/CMB-1988-013-8}}</ref> 

== Definition ==
Let <math>\ell^2</math> be the Hilbert space of square-summable sequences of [[complex number]]s, i.e., <math display="block">\ell^2 = \left\{ (a_0, a_1, a_2, \dots) : a_n \in \mathbb{C} \text{ and } \sum_{n=0}^\infty |a_n|^2 < \infty \right\}</math>The '''unilateral shift''' is the [[linear operator]] <math>S: \ell^2 \to \ell^2</math> defined by:
<math display=block>S(a_0, a_1, a_2, \dots) = (0, a_0, a_1, a_2, \dots)</math>This operator is also called the '''forward shift'''.

With respect to the standard [[orthonormal basis]] <math>(e_n)_{n=0}^\infty</math> for <math>\ell^2</math>, where <math>e_n</math> is the sequence with a 1 in the ''n''-th position and 0 elsewhere, the action of <math>S</math> is <math>Se_n = e_{n+1}</math>. Its [[matrix representation]] is:<math display="block">S = 
\begin{bmatrix}
0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & \cdots \\
1 & 0 & 0 & 0 & \cdots \\
0 & 1 & 0 & 0 & \cdots \\
0 & 0 & 1 & 0 & \cdots \\
\vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots
\end{bmatrix}
</math>This is a [[Toeplitz matrix|Toeplitz operator]] whose symbol is the function <math>f(z) = z</math>. It can be regarded as an infinite-dimensional [[Shift matrix|lower shift matrix]].

== Properties ==

=== Adjoint operator ===
The [[adjoint operator|adjoint]] of the unilateral shift, denoted <math>S^*</math>, is the '''backward shift'''. It acts on <math>\ell^2</math> as:
<math display="block">S^*(b_0, b_1, b_2, b_3, \dots) = (b_1, b_2, b_3, \dots)</math>The matrix representation of <math>S^*</math> is the [[conjugate transpose]] of the matrix for <math>S</math>:
<math display="block">S^* = 
\begin{bmatrix}
0 & 1 & 0 & 0 & \cdots \\
0 & 0 & 1 & 0 & \cdots \\
0 & 0 & 0 & 1 & \cdots \\
0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & \cdots \\
\vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots
\end{bmatrix}
</math>It can be regarded as an infinite-dimensional upper shift matrix.

=== Basic properties ===

* <math>S, S^*</math> are both continuous but not [[Compact operator|compact]].
* <math>S^*S = I</math>.
* <math>S, S^*</math> make up a pair of [[Unitary operator|unitary equivalence]] between <math>\ell^2</math> and the set of <math>\ell^2</math>-sequences whose first element is zero.

The [[resolvent operator]] has matrix representation<math display="block">(zI - S)^{-1} = 
\begin{bmatrix}
z^{-1} & 0 & 0 & 0 & \cdots \\
z^{-2} & z^{-1} & 0 & 0 & \cdots \\
z^{-3} & z^{-2} & z^{-1} & 0 & \cdots \\
z^{-4} & z^{-3} & z^{-2} & z^{-1} & \cdots \\
\vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots
\end{bmatrix}
</math>which is bounded iff <math>|z| > 1
</math>. Similarly, <math>(zI - S^*)^{-1} = ((z^*I - S)^{-1})^*
</math>.

For any <math>z \in \C, a \in \ell^2</math> with <math>\|a \| = 1
</math>,<math display="block">\|(zI - S) a\|^2 = 1 + |z|^2 - 2 \Re (\langle Sa, a \rangle z), \quad \|(zI - S^*) a\|^2 = 1-|a_0|^2 + |z|^2 - 2 \Re (\langle Sa, a \rangle z^*)
</math>where <math>\Re
</math> is the [[real part]].

=== Spectral theory ===
{{Math theorem
| name = Spectrum of the forward shift
| math_statement = Let <math>\mathbb{D}</math> be the open unit disk, <math>\overline{\mathbb{D}}</math> the closed unit disk, and <math>\mathbb{T}</math> the unit circle.
* The [[spectrum of an operator|spectrum]] of <math>S</math> is <math>\sigma(S) = \overline{\mathbb{D}}</math>.
* The [[point spectrum]] of <math>S</math> is empty: <math>\sigma_p(S) = \emptyset</math>.
* The [[approximate point spectrum]] of <math>S</math> is the unit circle: <math>\sigma_{ap}(S) = \mathbb{T}</math>.
}}
{{Math proof|title=Proof|proof=
To show <math>\sigma(S) = \overline{\mathbb{D}}</math>, use the matrix representation of <math>(zI-S)^{-1}
</math>, and note that it is bounded iff <math>|z| > 1
</math>.
To show <math>\sigma_p(S) = \emptyset
</math>, directly show that <math>S a = \lambda a
</math> implies <math>a = 0
</math>.

To show <math>\sigma_{ap}(S) = \mathbb T</math>, note that <math>\|(zI - S) a\|^2 \geq 1 + |z|^2 - 2|z| = (1-|z|)^2</math> for any <math>z \in \C, a \in \ell^2</math> with <math>\|a \| = 1
</math>, so <math>\sigma_{ap}(S) \subset  \overline{\mathbb{D}} \setminus \mathbb D = \mathbb T</math>. Conversely, for any <math>z \in \mathbb T</math>, construct the following unit vector<math display="block">a = \frac{1}{\sqrt N}(1, z^{-1}, z^{-2}, \dots, z^{-(N-1)}, 0, 0, \dots)</math>then <math>\|(zI - S) a\|^2 = 2/N</math>, which converges to 0 at <math>N \to \infty</math>.
}}

The spectral properties of <math>S^*</math> differ significantly from those of <math>S</math>:<ref name="GMR2023" />{{Reference page|location=Proposition 5.2.4}}
* <math>\sigma(S^*) = \overline{\mathbb{D}}</math> (since <math>\sigma(A^*) = \overline{\sigma(A)}</math>).
* The point spectrum <math>\sigma_p(S^*)</math> is the entire open unit disk <math>\mathbb{D}</math>. For any <math>\lambda \in \mathbb{D}</math>, the corresponding eigenvector is the geometric sequence <math>(1, \lambda, \lambda^2, \lambda^3, \dots)</math>.
* The approximate point spectrum <math>\sigma_{ap}(S^*)</math> is the entire closed unit disk <math>\overline{\mathbb{D}}</math>. To show this, it remains to show <math>\mathbb T \subset \sigma_{ap}(S^*) </math>, which can be proven by a similar construction as before, using <math>a = \frac{1}{\sqrt N}(1, z^{1}, z^{2}, \dots, z^{(N-1)}, 0, 0, \dots) </math>.

== Hardy space model ==
The unilateral shift can be studied using [[complex analysis]].

Define the [[H square|Hardy space]] <math>H^2</math> as the Hilbert space of [[analytic function]]s <math>f(z) = \sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n z^n</math> on the open unit disk <math>\mathbb{D}</math> for which the sequence of coefficients <math>(a_n)</math> is in <math>\ell^2</math>.

Define the [[multiplication operator]] <math>M_z</math> on <math>H^2</math>:
<math display="block">(M_z f)(z) = zf(z)</math>then <math>S </math> and <math>M_z </math> are unitarily equivalent via the [[unitary operator|unitary]] map <math>U: \ell^2 \to H^2</math> defined by<ref name="GMR2023" /><math display="block">U(a_0, a_1, a_2, \dots) = \sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n z^n</math>which gives <math>U^* M_z U = S </math>. Using this unitary equivalence, it is common in the literature to use <math>S</math> to denote <math>M_z</math> and to treat <math>H^2</math> as the primary setting for the unilateral shift.<ref name="GMR2023" />{{Reference page|location=Sec. 5.3}}

=== Commutant ===
The [[commutant]] of an operator <math>A</math>, denoted <math>\{A\}'</math>, is the [[Algebra over a field|algebra]] of all bounded operators that [[Commuting#In operator theory and quantum mechanics|commute]] with <math>A</math>. The commutant of the unilateral shift is the algebra of multiplication operators on <math>H^2</math> by bounded analytic functions.<ref name="GMR2023" />{{Reference page|location=Corollary 5.6.2}}<math display="block">\{S\}' = \{M_\varphi : \varphi \in H^\infty\}</math>Here, <math>H^\infty</math> is the space of bounded analytic functions on <math>\mathbb{D}</math>, and <math>(M_\varphi f)(z) = \varphi(z)f(z)</math>.

=== Cyclic vectors ===
A vector <math>x</math> is a [[cyclic vector]] for an operator <math>A</math> if the linear span of its orbit <math>\{A^n x : n \ge 0\}</math> is dense in the space. We have:<ref name="GMR2023" />{{Reference page|location=Sec. 5.7}}
* For the unilateral shift <math>S</math> on <math>H^2</math>, the cyclic vectors are the [[outer function]]s.
* A function <math>f \in H^2</math> that has a zero in the open unit disk <math>\mathbb{D}</math> is not a cyclic vector. This is because every function in the span of its orbit will also be zero at that point, so the subspace cannot be dense.
* A function <math>f \in H^2</math> that is bounded away from zero (i.e., <math>\inf_{z \in \mathbb{D}} |f(z)| > 0</math>) is a cyclic vector. 
* A function <math>f \in H^2</math>, that is in the open unit disk <math>\mathbb{D}</math> is nonzero but <math>\inf_{z \in \mathbb{D}} |f(z)| = 0</math>, may or may not be cyclic. For example, <math>f(z) = 1-z</math> is a cyclic vector.
The cyclic vectors are precisely the [[outer function]]s.

=== Lattice of invariant subspaces ===
The <math>S</math>-invariant subspaces of <math>H^2</math> are completely characterized analytically. Specifically, they are precisely <math>M_u(H^2)</math> where <math>u</math> is an [[inner function]].

The <math>S</math>-invariant subspaces make up a [[Linear subspace#Lattice of subspaces|lattice of subspaces]]. The two lattice operators, [[join and meet]], correspond to operations on inner functions.

Given two invariant subspaces <math>M_u(H^2), M_v(H^2)</math>, we have <math>M_u(H^2) \subset M_v(H^2)</math> iff <math>u/v \in H^2</math>.<ref name="GMR2023" />{{Reference page|location=Sec. 5.8}}
